questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code acquires and orders locks? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
Thread 1 calls transfer_credits(dir, "alice", "bob", 5) while thread 2 calls transfer_credits(dir, "bob", "alice", 7) at the same moment. What is the outcome?
choices: A deadlock is likely, because each thread locks its source principal first and then waits for the other thread's source
Both calls complete; std::scoped_lock acquires both mutexes without a lock-order cycle, so the transfers serialize
One call fails with SameAccount because the two ids overlap
Both calls complete only because the directory's shared_mutex serializes them

questions.prompt: transfer_credits looks up both principals through the directory and then locks them after find() has returned. What is the effect of that design?
choices: A principal removed from the directory between lookup and locking would cause a use-after-free
The directory lock is held for the whole transfer, which limits concurrency across unrelated accounts
Transfers never wait on the directory lock while holding a principal lock, and the shared_ptr copies keep both objects alive even if one is removed concurrently
Credits can be double-spent because the balance check happens before the lock is taken

questions.prompt: ids_with_role takes the directory's shared lock and then locks each principal's mutex in turn. Under what condition is this safe against deadlock with the other functions in this file?
choices: Only if no other thread ever calls create() or remove()
Only because shared_lock allows many readers, so readers never block each other
Whenever no code path acquires the directory lock while already holding a principal mutex, which holds for every function here
Only because lock_guard is released at the end of each loop iteration
